#845. Gonzalo García: ‘I love Craven Cottage – the fans can reach out and touch you’

Spain Under-21 striker admits the pace of the Premier League has surprised him but says he must stay calm over goal drought at Fulham

The first thing Rita Hayworth’s great nephew says when he walks in is: “Sorry I’m late.” Gonzalo García is not late, but it’s very like him: he is impeccably polite, accommodating, and there’s an almost gentle quality to him, a calm that’s not common but can help, especially in moments when the pressure builds. There’s a reason one of the coaches standing in the rain by the pitch where Spain’s under‑21s have just finished training says everyone here loves García. The Fulham striker shakes hands, introduces himself and ducks into the dressing room to change; then a few minutes later he’s back, apologising for a wait that wasn’t one.

Time to talk, so let’s start with Tinseltown, the family tale. García laughs. His great-aunt, born Margarita Carmen Cansino, was among the biggest stars in Hollywood, although he’s not sure he’s seen any of her films. His grandfather was a surgeon and others in the family followed. His uncles played rugby for Spain, but that wasn’t his thing. As for him, he enrolled in a degree in business management and analytics, and reckons he might have liked law, yet even that wasn’t his chosen field.

Hayworth’s family was from Seville province. “I know she was a great actress but I’m afraid I have to admit I’m not one for old films,” García concedes in an even tone. “My uncles played rugby for Ciencias and practically all of them were in the national team together. They tried to get me to play with my cousins, but I was always more into football.” He was good at it too: another Spain international, the Club World Cup’s top scorer, playing for Real Madrid.

Then this summer, with opportunities limited, he joined Fulham, his introductory interview conducted in impeccable English. Having joined Madrid aged 10, he was leaving home for the first time, as Fulham’s record signing, at 22. He had the language and intelligence to embrace it. As for being uprooted, he was used to that, growing up in Argentina and Chile as well as Spain.

“From very little my parents impressed upon me the importance of study, learning languages,” García says. “I’m at Villanueva university [in Madrid]. I started with dual honours business and analytics, although that became difficult with my profession. Now it’s just business, and I’m trying to arrange with the university how best to handle it [from London]. My parents considered it fundamental to speak English and I was always at international schools.

“Every two or three years we would change city. Obviously, there would be phases when I felt: ‘Pfff, again?!’ Having to move home because of my parents’ work. But I look back and feel grateful because, seen with perspective, it gives you opportunities to meet new people, see new places, learn. I’ve always had foreign friends with whom I spoke English.”

García has been joined at Fulham by César Palacios and Manuel Ángel from Madrid’s academy. Three 22-year-olds, like your very own Erasmus course. “Nah,” García says, laughing. “I wouldn’t call it an Erasmus because we’re talking about a big, ambitious career step. We’re grateful for the trust placed in us. I’ve been pleasantly surprised by London, a huge city with people from all nationalities and cultures and Fulham fit the situation I was in, the desire to grow.

“Álvaro Arbeloa explained the project, convinced me. I’d worked with him in Madrid. He knows me perfectly, how far he can push me. Equally, I know what he wants of me. That helps … [Arbeloa] told me it was a project that it will take time but that he needed me. I’m very, very happy. It’s one of the world’s best leagues, if not the best.”

And the toughest? Is English football as wild as it looks? “Yes!” García replies. “They had told me it was demanding, hard, but …” He cracks up. “I have to admit it still surprised me. That first game against Chelsea, I finished really, really tired. It was box to box, intense, a lot of running. Bit by bit I’m adapting. The intensity and pace is very different.

“Spain is more tactical, a bit more technical. English football is pace. You can’t lose concentration for a second, not a second. Anything can happen any moment. How many Premier League games are decided late? Suddenly there’s a goal in the 90th minute and again on 93. It’s your corner and their chance. The level of concentration, that constant transition, is what most sets the Premier League apart.”

Despite defeat on that opening day against Chelsea, García scored. A superb goal followed against AFC Wimbledon in the Carabao Cup. “It was super special to do it at Craven Cottage. I love how close the fans are – they can reach out and touch you. But I don’t consider myself someone who’s easily satisfied. I’m not like that. I always want more, more, more.”

García hasn’t scored since and Fulham went five league games without a win, pressure building. Which is where the calmness comes in. By the time they faced Hull, Arbeloa appeared on the edge of the sack, questions asked about his signings, García especially. Were three Madrid academy kids really what Fulham needed? Was the coach’s relationship with them not such a good thing after all?

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

No player is impermeable to what is said, García admits, but he insists: “We treat that as outside noise. And we all knew that the beginning wouldn’t be easy. There’s a change of cycle: the coach goes, a new coach comes, there are signings, a different system, idea. Everyone has to adapt: those already at the club and those of us who are new. We’re young too. Results weren’t going our way but we had good intentions: to play good football, build, apply the manager’s ideas bit by bit. We had to remain calm.”

Fulham go into Saturday’s game at Manchester City unbeaten in four in the league, the sense of them shifting towards something more pragmatic not shared by García. “I don’t think we changed anything against Hull,” he says of a game Fulham won 1-0. “We didn’t do anything we weren’t already doing. Nothing. Maybe we controlled the small details that hurt us but the idea was the same. The players were very clear what the manager asked, very firm: it was just a question of time. You have to be patient. If you watch Fulham, you see the manager’s idea: have the ball, construct attacks well, show maximum intensity constantly with and without the ball. Aggressive, ambitious.”

Chances are coming for García but goals aren’t. He has started every league game but not scored or assisted since the opening day. Yet if there is a sense of a man feeling the pressure, that’s not repeated here; instead there’s an evenness, an ease. And a smile when another, more welcome, stat is raised: he has made more off‑the‑ball runs into the area than anyone. Something to hold on to, perhaps, a process that will pay off. “Really?” he says. “Well, I’m happy for people to see that a striker can help the team without the ball. In the end, it’s about following the manager’s instructions.”

In the end, though, teams will be judged on results and strikers on goals, price too. He knows: this is what he does, the path he chose. “Pressure depends on how you look at it, really,” García says. “Football is [very psychological]. It happens fast: it doesn’t give you time to enjoy good moments or linger on bad ones. It’s a rollercoaster – up there, down here. It’s not flat, but you maintain balance, work daily, improve: go in, focus, repeat.

“It’s not that I don’t ‘care’ about the price, it’s that the market is the market; it doesn’t depend on me. Calmness always, perspective … I know strikers are measured by goals but, well, the days I don’t score I’m completely sure I will be able to walk off the pitch and say that, no matter what happened, I helped my team, doing a load of other things. It is what it is.”

It is also time. A head peers around the door, the bus is going. García holds out a hand, apologises again. “It’s been a pleasure,” he says.

#844. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

#843. Melania Trump Reveals Warning She Gave Son Barron Trump About Dating

President Donald Trump’s wife Melania Trump detailed the dating advice she gave their son Barron Trump, noting it’s a “dangerous world” so he should “be careful.”

Melania Trump is a special adviser for her son’s dating life.

The First Lady recalled the cautionary advice she gave her and President Donald Trump’s 20-year-old son Barron Trump when it came to his romantic life.

“I always say it’s a dangerous world out there,” Melania said in the Nov. 20 episode of her new Prime Video docuseries MELANIA, “and be careful.”

And beyond his dating life, the 56-year-old noted she’ll be there for Barron “anytime he wants to have my advice or input.”

“We have very open communication regarding life. I will always be there for him,” she continued. “I am, and I will always be. And he knows that he’s my priority, and he will always be my priority.”

Plus, as Melania quipped, “I'm a very cool mom to Barron, and I remind him all the time."

But while the former model has prioritized motherhood, she has been vocal about not strutting the path of parenthood alone. That’s why she was grateful to have her late mom Amalija Knavs, who died in 2024, to help raise Barron.

“My mother was the epitome of love and warmth, and for Barron, a grandmother who filled every moment with joy and wisdom,” Melania told USA Today in May. “Every story she read to Barron sparked his imagination, and every game they played strengthened their bond.”

Now, the Melania author is passing down the hard-earned advice she gained from raising Barron.

“To all the young mothers out there: Shower your children with love and support and always communicate openly,” she continued. “See them as their own unique individuals, not merely as extensions of yourself.”

And when it comes to ensuring a bright future for the next generation, Melania added, “Guide them with wisdom but establish a foundation of freedom where they can carve their own life path.”

For a closer look at the branches of Melania’s family tree, keep reading…

Ivana Trump was the first wife of President-elect Donald Trump. Born in Gottwaldov, Czechoslovakia—now Zlín of the Czech Republic—in 1949, she rose to fame as a competitive skier. And, thanks to her marriage to Austrian ski instructor Alfred Winklmayr in 1971, Ivana was able to travel often outside of Czechoslovakia.According to her book Raising Trump, the model met Donald three years after her 1973 divorce during a New York trip, where she'd traveled for a Canadian fashion show ahead of the Montreal Olympics. They wed in 1977 and welcomed three kids: Donald Trump Jr. born in 1977, Ivanka Trump born in 1981 and Eric Trump born in 1984.The pair's divorce was finalized in 1992 following his affair with Marla Maples, whom he later married. However, Ivana—who then married Riccardo Mazzucchelli for two years followed by Rossano Rubicondi for less than a year—and Donald remained on good terms.“Donald during the divorce was brutal,” she told ABC News in 2017. “He took the divorce as a business deal, and he cannot lose. He has to win. So he took about two years. And after the final situation was straightened up, we would just talk and we are friends.”Ivana died in 2022 at age 73. According to NBC News, the New York City Medical Examiner said she died of “blunt impact injuries” and that her manner of death was an accident. A senior NYC official with direct knowledge added the circumstances were consistent with a fall on the stairs in her New York apartment.

In 1977, Ivana and Donald welcomed their eldest son Donald Trump Jr. He graduated with a Bachelor’s degree in finance and real estate from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School in 2000 and began working for his father’s company The Trump Organization in 2001, where he now serves as the executive vice president. Don Jr. is also a director for both Trump Media & Technology Group Corp and PublicSquare Holdings and part of 1789 Capital firm. In addition, he's been involved in his dad’s political campaigns, including speaking at rallies and the Republican National Convention during his father's presidential runs.Don Jr. shares five children with his ex-wife, model Vanessa Haydon: Kai (who also made a speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention) Donald III, Tristan, Spencer and Chloe.Don Jr. was previously engaged to Fox News alum Kimberly Guilfoyle. However, he recently confirmed their split."Kimberly and I will never stop caring for each other," he told Page Six Dec. 13, "and will always keep a special bond."Don Jr. has since been linked to socialite Bettina Anderson. Four years after the arrival of Don Jr., Donald and Ivana became parents to daughter Ivanka Trump. Before her father’s presidency, the University of Pennsylvania alum worked at The Trump Organization. But after he was elected in 2016, the fashion brand founder—who had her own eponymous line—took on the role of Advisor to the President.After her dad announced he would be running for president again in 2024, Ivanka revealed she would be stepping out of the political arena to focus on her family with husband, former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner, and their children Arabella, Joseph and Theodore. “I love my father very much,” she said in part of a 2022 statement obtained by NBC News. “This time around, I am choosing to prioritize my young children and the private life we are creating as a family. I do not plan to be involved in politics.”

Born in 1984, Eric Trump is the third child of Ivana and Donald. He graduated with a degree in finance and management from Georgetown University.Like his brother, Eric works as executive vice president of The Trump Organization, which he joined in 2007. He is also president of Trump Winery.Eric is married to Republican National Committee co-chair Lara Trump, with whom he shares kids Luke and Carolina.

Marla Maples is Donald’s second wife, whom he met while still married to Ivana.

In Raising Trump, Ivana wrote the actress approached her about the affair during a trip to Aspen in 1989. Still, Marla said on a 2018 episode of the ABC podcast Journeys of Faith with Paula Faris that she “never considered” herself a mistress. "My intention was to never bring hurt," she continued. "Do I wish more than anything that we could have had this relationship after his divorce papers were signed? Absolutely. I mean, with all my heart. How much heartache would it have saved so many people if I had seen that piece of paper before we got involved? But it didn't happen that way." Marla and Donald welcomed daughter Tiffany Trump in 1993, and the couple wed later that year. However, the Dancing With the Stars alum and the 47th commander in chief announced their separation four years later and finalized their divorce in 1999.

After her parents’ breakup, Tiffany Trump relocated with her mother to California. "She moved us out of New York to get out of the spotlight and let me grow up and find my own identity versus being in the shadow of a name or growing up very young with all that pressure,” Tiffany told People in 2016. “So, she wanted me to have a chance to have a normal childhood. I think that she did well in that.” She released her 2011 single “Like a Bird" and graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 2016 with a B.A. in sociology, focusing on law and society. She then went to Georgetown Law School, where she graduated with a JD in 2020. In 2022, Tiffany wed Michael Boulos. Her father announced they're expecting their first baby during an October 2024 speech at the Detroit Economic Club. "She’s an exceptional young woman," he said during his remarks. "And she’s going to have a baby. So that’s nice.”The little one made his debut on May 15, 2025."Welcome to the world our sweet baby boy, Alexander Trump Boulos," Tiffany wrote on X on his birthday. "We love you beyond words! Thank you for coming into our lives!"

Melania Trump is Donald’s third wife and current First Lady of the United States. Born in Mesto, Slovenia in 1970, she is the second First Lady to be born outside of the U.S. and the only First Lady to become a naturalized U.S. citizen.Melania met Donald in New York in 1996 while she was working as a model. “It was a big fashion party that my friend organized, fashion week, and he invited me,” she recalled on a 2016 episode of On the Record With Greta Van Susteren. “That’s how we met with Donald.” Melania and Donald married in 2005, and they welcomed son Barron Trump the following year. In 2024, she released her memoir Melania and she's set to appear in a documentary. Melania has also spoken about where she will spend her time during her husband's second presidency.

"I will be in the White House," she told Fox & Friends in an interview that aired Jan. 13. "When I need to be in New York, I will be in New York. When I need to be in Palm Beach, I will be in Palm Beach. My first priority is to be a mom, to be a first lady, to be a wife. And once we're in on January 20, you serve the country."

Born in 2006, Barron Trump is Donald and Melania’s only child. While he has lived a more private life—relocating with his parents from New York to live in Washington, D.C. and then Florida—it looked like he might enter the political world after he was selected in May 2024 as a Florida delegate to the Republican National Convention. However, Barron declined the offer."While Barron is honored to have been chosen as a delegate by the Florida Republican Party,” a statement from Melania’s office shared with NBC News at the time said, “he regretfully declines to participate due to prior commitments.”Like studying, perhaps, with Barron starting his freshman year at New York University in 2024. "He was accepted to a lot of colleges," his father told the Daily Mail in an interview published Sept. 4. #842. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#841. Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet

The 30-year-old former England star combines Twitch streaming with working to return to the top as a player

Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.

“We’ll do maybe two days on, one day off, and then three days on, one day off,” says Peters. “We’ve been doing that for just over a year now. It’s full-on. It’s pretty much as if you were at a club.”

Dele rose as a teenager to a level of stardom few experience and, used to media attention, doesn’t mind that his absence from football draws scrutiny. But he disagrees with the suggestion that choosing to stream on Twitch is a sign he has lost interest in the game that made him wealthy enough to never need to work again.

To a modest Twitch audience, he sometimes plays video games, sometimes just talks. He has a knack for creating viral content, sharing a phone call with Harry Kane and playing a game of EA Sports FC with IShowSpeed, one of the most famous online influencers. When he lost that game – and a bet – he wore an Arsenal shirt, apologising to Spurs fans before burning it. When TalkSport pundits claimed Dele was wasting his potential by becoming a streamer, Dele responded in a live stream, pointing out he was recording himself in his spare time and if he was out at nightclubs, it would be worse. Even then he was polite.

“When people see him online streaming or whatever he does in his private time, the initial thought is: ‘He’s done with football, then,’” Peters says. “He’s been training for a year and a half by himself. If he was done with football he wouldn’t be doing that. His actions show that the hunger is still there. A lot of people would come out of the game and then stop and lose the hunger for it, but he’s still chipping away every day, trying to get back and get to somewhere that he’s happy with.”

Dele broke through at MK Dons as a slight but devilish defensive midfielder, dominating League One midfields full of hardened professionals, before being scouted by Tottenham. Mauricio Pochettino attended MK Dons’ 4-0 League Cup win against Manchester United in 2014 and saw enough to leave early and convince Daniel Levy to pay £5m.

By the time Dele turned 21, his statistics were superior to Cristiano Ronaldo’s at the same age: 26 goals and 14 assists to Ronaldo’s 14 and 13. His 40 goal involvements equalled Frank Lampard, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham combined at the same age.

“He’s scored more in his first 50 league games than Steven Gerrard, Wayne Rooney and Frank Lampard,” Pochettino wrote in his book Brave New World. “He may go on to be better than all of them because he has the quality; now he just needs consistency.”

But there were, perhaps, warning signs of what would happen at Spurs. One source who worked closely with Dele describes him as a “cheeky chappy”; charming and universally popular.

He wasn’t one to miss training, but there were concerns he wasn’t leading the pristine lifestyle of many elite players, and tabloid stories about his private life trailed him. Pochettino was concerned when he saw Dele’s WhatsApp photo, a cartoon of a boy surrounded by people wanting a piece of him, believing he needed support from the right people. John McDermott, the head of coaching and development, said: “When the trough is full, the pigs come from all over to feed.”

When Dele voluntarily liquidated one of his companies this month, documents showed an estimated surplus after costs of £7.6m, suggesting the 30-year-old has not squandered the millions he earned at his peak in wages and sponsorship agreements, including a five-year deal with Adidas. He also owns a property portfolio worth more than £1.5m.

In the early days Pochettino warned Dele about the danger of not giving maximum effort in matches and training, a sentiment later shared by José Mourinho when he became Spurs manager. “I think one day you will regret, if you don’t reach what you can reach,” Mourinho told Dele in his office as Amazon Prime’s cameras rolled.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although Dele formed a formidable relationship with Kane on the pitch, and was twice named the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s young player of the year while playing behind the striker, he was closer to Eric Dier off it. And perhaps it was those anchors – Pochettino and Dier – that Dele lost later in his career.

His time with Pochettino was fondly remembered. For the Argentinian’s 50th birthday celebrations, Dele recorded a heartfelt video for his former manager. “The message was beautiful,” says one party-goer.

In almost five years since leaving Spurs, he has made one league start at Everton and 10 at Besiktas, before a loan at Como, where Cesc Fàbregas tried to rediscover the player he once was. He came off the bench once and was sent off nine minutes later.

Dele, according to those close to him, is biding his time to get his next move right. He will be 31 in April and wants a suitable contract. He has spoken to a host of clubs, with interest from the Premier League and the Championship, and from the Middle East, where he has been tempted by the riches of the Saudi Pro League, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. There has also been interest from Major League Soccer and he has held talks with clubs in Brazil and Japan. It is believed he will join a club this season.

In preparation, Peters is also guiding Dele’s nutrition, though he does not require much guidance. “Del’s a weird one, because he doesn’t snack, he doesn’t eat unhealthily, he doesn’t have a Sprite or a Coke or whatever. He’s never really been that kind of guy. All he does is drink coconut water, and he’ll have a small lunch, or his cheat day will be a Nando’s or something.”

Happiness is his priority. He spoke candidly on Gary Neville’s The Overlap in 2023 about his struggles with mental health and an addiction to sleeping pills after revealing abuse as a child. “Because he’s had such a long time out, he’s like: ‘What’s another few months if it means that I’m going to find something I’m actually happy with?’” Peters says. The aim is to “carry on for as long as possible”.

For the time being, Dele’s days are simple. When not training, he goes for coffee or a swim, and he has taken up padel. “He’s very much a person that’s happy with the little things,” Peters says. “He’s always the person that’s positive, the one that, if the group’s down or whatever, is going to pick everyone up. He’s happy with what he’s doing. His main happiness is playing football, and that’s what he wants to do.”

#840. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

#839. Golloria Responds to Huda Beauty’s Apology for Removing Darkest Powder

Beauty influencer Golloria responded to Huda Beauty founder Huda Kattan's apology for how the company handled removing its darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle.

Golloria can’t conceal her thoughts on Huda Beauty’s apology.

After the makeup brand’s founder Huda Kattan apologized to the beauty influencer for how her company handled discontinuing their darkest setting powder Coffee Cake and replacing it with Coco Truffle, Golloria shared her thoughts on the response.

“I appreciate your apology and you taking the time to get back to me,” Golloria posted in the comments of Kattan’s Nov. 20 Instagram post. “Speaking from both my experience as a shade consultant and as a dark skinned woman whose shade options are directly affected by this decision, I don’t think Coco Truffle should replace Coffee Cake. And that’s just the honest truth.”

The TikToker explained that she heard Huda Beauty’s reasoning that Coffee Cake wasn’t doing well with consumers, but added that she didn’t think the two shades were “interchangeable,” noting that “a shade occupying a similar depth in a range doesn’t necessarily mean it serves the same complexions.”

“You’ve said several times that you want to better serve dark skinned women, and part of that is listening to the women telling you that Coffee Cake already works for them,” the 25-year-old continued. “That feedback should help guide what you preserve as you expand the range.”

She also added that darker skinned women “deserve variety in both depth and undertone,” and that having both shades would help create that inclusion. Instead, Golloria shared in her own Instagram caption that she felt Huda Beauty was “doing what's easiest for the brand instead of what's needed by the women you say you want to serve.”

“Inclusion means making room for our differences,” she wrote, “not asking us to settle for whatever is most convenient for you to offer.”

As for Kattan, while the beauty founder did not reply to Golloria’s comment, she explained in her apology video that she was sorry for how the conversation about the shade replacement had been handled with Golloria, especially as it was happening during a busy time for the brand and when Kattan herself had to undergo emergency surgery for a ruptured breast implant in April.

According to the 43-year-old, her team found that Coffee Cake was “not something that a lot of people have shared positive feedback with us on,” adding that they “definitely thought we could make it a lot better.”

The decision led them to launching Coco Truffle as a replacement for Coffee Cake, first as a pressed powder, then as a loose powder—although it was not yet widely available.. But after hearing from their consumers, Kattan realized they should have done a better job being more inclusive with their shades.

“Inclusivity is not about, ‘Yes, done, check, we're inclusive.’ That to me is some of the things that are wrong with the industry,” she said. “It's 2026. We can do better. We can do better and I think brands should be doing better in 2026.”

And while they will be reworking Coco Truffle to make sure it’s available “as quickly as possible,” she also regretted fully removing Coffee Cake from their lineup.

“We should have kept it in stores,” Kattan said, “because at the end of the day, if some people liked it, we should have kept it in stores until there was something better available.”

She also once again apologized for not having better communicated all of this to Golloria initially, although she was hopeful that the beauty influencer and Huda Beauty fans would appreciate Coco Truffle.

“I'm hoping to give you guys a shade that you guys really, really love, and all the beautiful rich skin tone girls and boys feel really represents them,” Kattan shared, “and is perfect for their skin tone.”

#838. Liverpool fan found not guilty of racial abuse after Antoine Semenyo withdraws from case

Man accused of abusing former Bournemouth winger

Alleged incident happened at Anfield game in 2025

A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the Manchester City forward withdrew his support for the prosecution.

Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool magistrates court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the Premier League match between Liverpool and Semenyo’s former club Bournemouth at Anfield on 15 August last year.

But Simon Jones, prosecuting, said: “Following recent contact made with Mr Semenyo, he has indicated he is no longer supportive of proceedings and the prosecution do not consider it is appropriate to compel him. In those circumstances we offer no further evidence in the case.”

District judge Mary Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty to the charge of racially aggravated behaviour.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Semenyo, who left Bournemouth for Manchester City in January, had been due to give evidence last month but the trial was adjourned halfway through when Mogan was taken to hospital after a seizure.

The court had heard Mogan, in a wheelchair, shouted racial abuse at Semenyo as he went to take a throw-in about 30 minutes into the game. He was alleged to have said: “Hurry up and take the throw-in, you black bastard.”

Opening the case last month, Mr Jones said: “That racial abuse was shouted directly at Antoine Semenyo, who was close to him. Mr Semenyo briefly froze, as he couldn’t believe what the male had said.”

Mogan then shouted: “I’m talking to you, you cunt,” the court heard. Witnesses also said they saw him throw his chewing gum at the footballer.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Semenyo reported the incident to the referee and Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time. Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police in interview that Semenyo had called him a cripple after he shouted at the player to “hurry up”.

Mogan declined to comment as he left court.

#837. When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June
